verses.text: So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants, and stewards of God’s mysteries.
Here, moreover, it is required of stewards, that they be found faithful.
But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by man’s judgment. Yes, I don’t judge my own self.
For I know nothing against myself. Yet I am not justified by this, but he who judges me is the Lord.

Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and reveal the counsels of the hearts. Then each man will get his praise from God.

Now these things, brothers, I have in a figure transferred to myself and Apollos for your sakes, that in us you might learn not to think beyond the things which are written, that none of you be puffed up against one another.
For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?
You are already filled. You have already become rich. You have come to reign without us. Yes, and I wish that you did reign, that we also might reign with you.
For, I think that God has displayed us, the apostles, last of all, like men sentenced to death. For we are made a spectacle to the world, both to angels and men.
We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You have honor, but we have dishonor.
Even to this present hour we hunger, thirst, are naked, are beaten, and have no certain dwelling place.
We toil, working with our own hands. When people curse us, we bless. Being persecuted, we endure.
Being defamed, we entreat. We are made as the filth of the world, the dirt wiped off by all, even until now.
I don’t write these things to shame you, but to admonish you as my beloved children.
For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, yet not many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News.
I beg you therefore, be imitators of me.
Because of this I have sent Timothy to you, who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, who will remind you of my ways which are in Christ, even as I teach everywhere in every assembly.
Now some are puffed up, as though I were not coming to you.
But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing. And I will know, not the word of those who are puffed up, but the power.
For God’s Kingdom is not in word, but in power.
What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?

footnotes.content: Paul calls us to see his role—and any leader's role—not as someone to elevate, but as Christ's servant, caring for things belonging to God. A good manager of household treasures doesn't imagine the treasures are theirs. What a relief that leadership is supposed to be stewardship, not stardom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A steward's one job is to be faithful. Not to be liked, not to be impressive—faithful. I've seen people ruin their peace trying to impress others, when all that was ever required was quiet obedience to the one who hired them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul says judgment by mere humans doesn't bother him much. He's learned that other people's opinions—even wrong ones—are not the measure of him. That's hard to learn, but once you do, you're freed from exhausting yourself trying to prove your worth to whoever's watching.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even a clean conscience isn't enough to justify you; only the Lord who sees everything can do that. There's something beautiful in that—no amount of your own good feelings about yourself can settle the real question, and no accusation can destroy you either. Only He judges.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul names a real day: the Lord comes and brings light to hidden things, reveals the heart's counsels, and then—praise from God. At resurrection, all our confused guessing about each other ends. Until then, we're wise to hold our judgments lightly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul uses himself and Apollos as examples—live lessons—so the Corinthians can learn not to go beyond what's written. When we add our own opinions to Scripture and boast about following a leader's spin, we're swollen with pride. He's trying to keep them humble and biblically grounded.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every good thing you have came to you; you received it. So what's there to boast about? You're already full of His gifts, and somehow some of you act like you earned it or deserve praise for it. Paul's cutting right through pride with a quiet question.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Corinthians are boasting as if they've already inherited the kingdom in full glory—filled, rich, reigning. Paul's tone is almost wry: 'I wish it were true, so we apostles could share your triumph.' He's showing them their spiritual immaturity by their own words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God has placed the apostles last—like condemned men in a Roman amphitheater—a spectacle to the watching cosmos. While the Corinthians think they're already victorious, Paul and the apostles are living the road of kenosis, emptying, visible to angels and people alike.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The reversal is stark: the apostles are fools, weak, dishonored; the Corinthians reckon themselves wise, strong, and honored. Paul isn't complaining—he's pointing out that you can't have both the kingdom of the world and the kingdom of Christ at the same time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hunger, thirst, nakedness, beatings, no place to sleep—this is not poetry. This is Paul's present, ongoing reality. He's not asking for pity; he's showing them what faithfulness costs. The Corinthians should see in his life where the real courage and dependence on Christ truly reside.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Working with his own hands, blessing those who curse him, enduring persecution—Paul is living out the Beatitudes in real time. He's not preaching at them from comfort; he's showing them what it looks like when you follow Jesus when the world is against you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Defamed, treated as scum of the earth, the dirt cleaned off everyone's shoes—yet Paul speaks of it plainly, without self-pity. There's a quiet strength in that inventory. He's not just surviving; he's witnessing to the Corinthians that glory and shame are not the final word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After laying out all that hardship, Paul says: I'm not trying to shame you. I'm talking like a father who loves his children and wants them to grow up. That's why the hard words—not to destroy, but to call them toward maturity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They have many tutors in Christ, but not many fathers. Paul became their father by bringing them the Gospel. There's real tenderness here—a fathering love that carries authority but also deep care. Not all teachers father; some just transfer information.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In light of everything—his weaknesses, sufferings, humble love—Paul asks them to imitate him. He's not asking for blind allegiance; he's asking them to watch how a man follows Jesus through difficulty and learn to do the same.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Timothy is Paul's beloved son in the Lord, sent to remind the Corinthians of Paul's ways in Christ. This is a real messenger, a real person, carrying the embodied example of how the apostle lives and teaches. Not a doctrine, but a life lived.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Some Corinthians are puffed up, thinking Paul won't come back to check on them. They're boasting as if his absence gives them permission to do as they please. Paul's visit will be a reality check.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul will come soon if the Lord wills, and when he does, he won't listen to their fine words—he'll know the power that's actually in them. Talk is easy; the real presence of Christ's power in a life is unmistakable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The kingdom of God doesn't rest on our clever speech. It rests on power—the power to transform a human heart, to make a slave free, to make death swallow defeat. Words are just the shell; power is the living truth inside.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul leaves it to them: Do you want me to come with a rod of correction, or with love and gentleness? The choice reflects what they need. A wise father knows when to be firm and when to comfort. He's ready to be either, depending on whether they've learned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
